scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The imported Angevin Empire polygon spans 1200 to 1279 and includes lands lost much earlier. It is retained as unverified imported geometry, with dates explicitly labeled map coverage. The narrative gives independently sourced earlier acquisition and later disintegration; no single exact empire-ending year is invented.

The Angevin Empire is a modern collective label for dynastic dominions, not a claim that all territories had one law, language, status or uniform administration. The card avoids the source’s expansive superlative about being the largest European empire of the age.

English Heritage’s concise origin account simplifies the transmission of Normandy through Henry’s parents. The card says Henry acquired Normandy and Anjou rather than relying on a stronger unsupported claim about a particular deed of inheritance.

Wharram Percy is a regional English example, not a model of every village in Aquitaine or Normandy. The pre-thirteenth-century timber evidence and mill sequence are kept separate from later medieval stone longhouses, gaming pieces and spindle whorls, which are not projected backward without object-level dating.

Dover’s ceremonial and pilgrim functions are explicitly interpretive. The tower’s modern rooms are not presented as preserved medieval furnishings. No archaeological examination or physical visit by the researcher is claimed.

The Limoges reliquary is the British Museum object described by Naomi Speakman, dated about 1210. The museum catalogue also offers circa 1200 to 1210; the card follows the exhibition dating and marks it approximate. Museum arrival in 1878 is not treated as an excavation or production date. Descriptions come from the written catalogue; its photographs were not independently inspected.

The town history dates Château-Gaillard’s construction 1196 to 1198 and capture March 6, 1204. It distinguishes mainland Normandy from the Channel Islands. The card does not repeat its absolute statement that every excluded refugee died without reconciling siege narratives.

The pipe-roll guide returned HTTP 403 on direct web opening. Only its indexed introductory text was used, for the 1129 to 1130 roll and continuous series from 1155; no particular account, amount, sheriff or financial transaction is invented.

The Assize of Clarendon was read in the 1915 translation hosted by the Internet Medieval Sourcebook. Its jurors presented accusations; they are not equated with a modern trial jury. Prescriptive clauses are not treated as comprehensive observations of actual implementation.
The 1166 Assize is distinct from the Constitutions of Clarendon of 1164. No claim is made that Henry invented every component of English common law or that ordeals met modern standards of justice.

Magna Carta’s 1215 settlement, subsequent reissues and the surviving 1297 document are separated. The NARA page’s broad statement about the king personally affixing a seal is not repeated, and a single universally signed original is not implied.

No successor link is added because the divided territorial outcome and matching event-year geometry have not been verified. Independent historical review, identity, chronology, geometry and depth assessment remain pending.
